title: The Second Start of Onsi Sawiris, Years After Egypt Took His Firm
dek: After Nasser nationalised his firm, Onsi Sawiris worked in Libya for years, then came home in the mid-1970s and began again with a handful of staff.

story.event: Returning from Libya to restart in contracting after his first company was nationalised
story.summary: Onsi Sawiris's road and canal contracting firm was partly nationalised in 1961 and later fully taken over as El Nasr Civil Works; he stayed on for about five years, left for Libya in 1966 and built contracting work there. In the mid-1970s, as Sadat opened Egypt's economy, he returned and founded Orascom with a handful of staff, the start of what became one of Egypt's largest business groups.
paragraphs: For about five years after 1961, Onsi Sawiris went to work at a contracting company that was no longer his. He had founded it in the early 1950s, after a short spell farming his family's land in Sohag that, he later said, taught him the peasants knew more about farming than he did. The firm paved roads and dug irrigation canals and grew into one of Egypt's larger contractors. Under Gamal Abdel Nasser it was partly nationalised in 1961 and fully taken over later, becoming El Nasr Civil Works. Sawiris stayed on to run it for the state; one company history says he was not allowed to leave Egypt until 1966.

When he could leave, he went to Libya and built up contracting work there, while his wife and three sons stayed behind in Egypt. He later said he was in Libya for twelve years and that the most important thing he learned there was "how to haggle down prices." Of his wife he said that she "witnessed with me very harsh days after the nationalization." He kept paying for his sons' education: Naguib went on to study in Zurich, Samih in Berlin and Nassef at the University of Chicago.

By the mid-1970s two things had changed. President Anwar Sadat was dismantling Nasser's socialist policies and opening the economy to private business, and relations between Libya and Egypt were souring. Sawiris chose to go back to the country that had taken his first company and to start again in the same trade. Sources give 1975, 1976 or 1977 for the founding of Orascom; a company history says it began with five employees, while a tribute from Cairo's Coptic Orthodox Cultural Centre says three, in two rooms and a hall. The company history adds that he was struggling to pay his sons' fees.

Orascom grew with the economy that followed, and his sons joined once their studies were done. In the 1980s and 1990s the group moved into tourism, computer services and mobile telephones, and by the mid-1990s, Bloomberg reported, it was one of Egypt's largest private builders. His sons went on to run its telecoms, hotel and construction arms. When Onsi Sawiris died in 2021, aged 90, he was the patriarch of Egypt's richest business family.

quote.text: There is surely no greater wisdom, than well to time the beginnings, and onsets, of things.
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Sawiris did not choose when his first company was taken from him. He did choose when to begin the second, once Sadat was reopening the economy. Bacon ranks that kind of timing above everything else a person can bring to a new venture.

reflection: Sawiris lost a company he had built, then spent years running it for someone else and more years working away from his family. What he brought home was skill, a habit of bargaining hard and a few people willing to start again in a small office.

A setback can make the next beginning feel either urgent or impossible. Bacon's point is that timing deserves as much care as effort. If something you care about has stalled, it may not need more force this week. It may need you to watch the conditions honestly, and to notice when they have really changed.
invitation: Think of one plan you set aside after a setback. Write down what has changed since then, around you or in you, and what would still need to change before you pick it up again.

sources.title: Onsi Sawiris, head of Egypt's richest business family, dies at 90
sources.supports: Born 1930 in Sohag; farming after graduation and his television remark that peasants knew more about farming than he did; founding a company building roads and digging canals; partial nationalisation in 1961 and full state takeover in 1965; moving to Libya in 1966; his remark 'I was in Libya for 12 years' and that he learned 'how to haggle down prices'; return in the 1970s as Sadat dismantled Nasser's socialist policies; creating Orascom; diversification into tourism, computer services and telecommunications in the 1980s and 1990s; died aged 90, head of Egypt's richest business family.

sources.title: Onsi Sawiris, influential patriarch of Egypt's billionaire dynasty, dies at 90
sources.publisher: Bloomberg, published by Gulf News (29 June 2021)
sources.supports: Construction firm founded in 1950 that grew into one of Egypt's largest contractors building roads and waterways; nationalised by Nasser in 1961 and renamed El Nasr Civil Works Company; a new contracting business in Libya; return in the 1970s as Libyan-Egyptian relations soured; Orascom among Egypt's largest private builders by the mid-1990s; sons leading the telecoms, hotels and construction companies.

sources.title: Orascom Construction Industries S.A.E. (International Directory of Company Histories)
sources.supports: Founding in 1950 and public-works contracts by the late 1950s; nationalisation as Nasr Civil Works; Sawiris losing his passport and working as an employee of the company he had founded until given his passport in 1966; wife and sons remaining in Egypt while he went to Libya; sons' studies in Zurich, Berlin and Chicago; return and founding of Orascom Construction in 1977 'from almost nothing, with just five employees' while he struggled to pay for his sons' education; sons joining the business.

sources.title: Sawiris family head, billionaire Onsi, dies at age 91
sources.supports: The contracting company 'Onsi and Lamie' paving roads and digging irrigation canals; partial nationalisation in 1961, later full; Sawiris remaining its head for five years; emigration to Libya in 1966; return in the mid-1970s and the founding of Orascom General Contracting and Trade by 1976.

sources.title: Onsi Sawiris: Upper Egyptian businessperson who rebuilt his empire after nationalisation
sources.supports: First commercial registry in 1952; nationalisation as Al-Nasr Civil Works; wife and three children left in Egypt while he worked in Libya; return after 12 years under Sadat; founding of Orascom General Contracting and Trading in 1975 after Sadat's open-door policy.

cross_checks.claim: Sawiris's contracting firm was nationalised under Nasser from 1961 and became El Nasr Civil Works
He stayed on at the nationalised company for about five years before leaving for Libya in 1966
His wife and sons stayed in Egypt while he worked in Libya
He returned in the mid-1970s, under Sadat's economic opening, and founded Orascom (dated 1975, 1976 or 1977)
Orascom started very small (three or five employees)

research_notes: Dates disagree. First company: 1950 (Bloomberg, IDCH, Xinhua) or a first commercial registry in 1952 (Daily News Egypt, Family Business Histories); the story says 'the early 1950s'. Nationalisation: partial in 1961 and full in 1965 (The National); Bloomberg says nationalised in 1961; the story says partly in 1961 and fully later. Orascom's founding: 1975 (Daily News Egypt), 1976 (Egypt Independent, Xinhua, Family Business Histories, Daily News Egypt 2015), 1977 (IDCH); the story gives all three. Libya: Sawiris said he was there twelve years, which from 1966 would mean about 1978, later than most founding dates; the Coptic Orthodox Cultural Center says twelve years 'until the mid-seventies'. The story reports his own figure as his and dates the return to the mid-1970s. Reasons for returning: The National and Daily News Egypt point to Sadat's economic opening; Bloomberg says Libyan-Egyptian relations soured; IDCH ties the return to the Camp David accords, which it dates to 1976, but the accords were signed in 1978, so that link is not used. Staff at the restart: five employees (IDCH) against three, in 'two rooms and a hall' (Coptic Orthodox Cultural Center); the story gives both with their sources. His role after nationalisation: 'remained its head' (Egypt Independent, the Cultural Center) or 'executive manager' (Family Business Histories) against 'forced to work as an employee' with his passport taken (IDCH); the story says he stayed on to run it for the state and attributes the passport claim to the company history. A WebFetch summary of the IDCH page wrongly said his family later joined him in Libya; the page itself says they remained in Egypt, as Daily News Egypt and Family Business Histories also say. The quotes from Sawiris come from a television interview quoted by The National and from words quoted by the Cultural Center; neither gives the interview's date. Age at death is given as 90 (The National, Bloomberg) or 91 (Egypt Independent, Daily News Egypt); the story uses 90. Funding is classed as bootstrapped: no source mentions outside capital for the restart, and the IDCH says it began 'from almost nothing'. Al-Ahram's obituary and Arab News were blocked. The Bacon quotation's locator follows the essay numbering of the 1625 edition, in which 'Of Delays' is Essay 21.
